growth_story.headline: New Zealand's income per person has grown slowly but steadily since 1990; a post-pandemic slump has left it 3.2 percent below its 2022 peak.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 the data show one long era: income per person grew about 1.3 percent a year over 1990-2025, with no lasting shift up or down. The era opened with a deep fall in 1991 (-5.8 percent), after reforms that began in the mid-1980s, and a strong rebound from 1993 (5.2 percent); IMF staff later described growth in the decade after 1993 as much improved. Growth then cooled: income per person fell in 2008 and 2009, the OECD notes that productivity has slowed since that crisis, and the average dropped from 1.0 percent a year over 2006-2015 to 0.7 over 2016-2025. After a dip in 2020 (-2.2 percent) the economy bounced back in 2021 and 2022 (4.0 and 3.4 percent), and the OECD says this expansion outran capacity and pushed up inflation. Sharp interest-rate rises then slowed the economy while record migration lifted the population, so income per person fell three years running, from 2023 to 2025. In 2025 it was 3.2 percent below its 2022 peak and about where it first was in 2019.

threads.title: Reforms and the 1990s rebound
threads.text: Wide reforms from the mid-1980s came with slow growth, and income per person fell 5.8 percent in 1991 before rising 5.2 percent in 1993. IMF staff found that growth improved markedly in the decade after 1993, yet income per person still had not caught up with richer OECD countries.

threads.title: Slow productivity growth
threads.text: The OECD dates a slowdown in productivity to the 2008 global financial crisis, and labour productivity remains weak next to other rich countries. The OECD lists a small home market, shallow capital markets, distance and high energy costs among the things weighing on investment and productivity, and the IMF points to low capital per worker and limited innovation.

threads.title: Post-pandemic boom, then tightening
threads.text: After the 2020 dip the economy bounced back faster than it could supply, and inflation rose. The central bank raised interest rates quickly, and investment and spending slowed, which lines up with income per person falling from 2023.

threads.title: Migration and income per person
threads.text: Record migration in 2023 kept total output growing while income per person fell, because the population grew faster than the economy. Net migration then dropped sharply from its late-2023 peak, slowing growth in the number of workers.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a recovery under way from late 2025, but the data show income per person still slipping in 2025 (-0.2 percent), 3.2 percent below its 2022 peak. In 2023 the sources stress that migration kept total output growing, while income per person fell. The two can both be true because the population grew faster than the economy.
